query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In phosphorus-containing high‐entropy alloys, a controlled minor similar-element substitution that narrows the atomic size distribution can improve glass‐forming ability and enhance the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
generation.material_initial_state: Phosphorus-containing high‐entropy or compositionally complex alloys produced via rapid cooling that yield a partially amorphous structure with significant lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low-level substitution of one transition metal with another element of similar chemical character but slightly different atomic radius (thereby fine-tuning the δ′ parameter) during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: When the alloy is processed under rapid cooling conditions that typically induce an amorphous phase; the effect is expected when substitution levels are minor (e.g., less than 10%) and the replacement element has a close chemical behavior. In contrast, under slow cooling conditions or with high substitution levels, the expected benefits may not manifest.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced lattice distortion and a more uniform atomic size distribution in the amorphous matrix.
generation.mechanism: Lowering lattice distortion decreases the density of heterogeneous nucleation sites for crystallization, thereby stabilizing the disordered (amorphous) structure during thermal exposure. This controlled adjustment of interatomic spacing diminishes the driving force for phase separation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to exhibit a broader processing window for achieving a fully amorphous state and a higher onset temperature for crystallization on heating, relative to the baseline alloy without substitution.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high‐entropy alloys processed under identical conditions but without any similar-element substitution.
generation.boundary: This improvement is projected under conditions where the substitution percentage is kept low and the substitute element is carefully chosen to minimize chemical disruption. Excess substitution or inappropriate elemental choices could negate the effect or even promote crystallization.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the improvement in glass-forming ability and thermal stability is uncertain and may vary with exact compositional adjustments and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys: one with the proposed minor similar-element substitution and one control set without substitution. Process each set by identical rapid cooling methods. Then, conduct differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), X-ray diffraction, and transmission electron microscopy to compare the amorphous content and the crystallization onset temperature.
measurements: X-ray diffraction to quantify amorphous versus crystalline phase fractions
DSC to determine glass transition and crystallization onset temperatures
Transmission electron microscopy for detailed microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in overall amorphous content or an upward shift in the crystallization onset temperature compared to the control, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Separating the Role of Mixing‐Entropy on the Dynamics of Glass‐Forming Liquids

Abstract: AbstractWhile the concept of high entropy has gained prominence in materials design, disentangling specific impacts of entropy on material properties from the enthalpy of mixing remains elusive. It is demonstrated that the role of entropy can be distinguished from the dynamics of glass‐forming liquids through micro‐alloying. Based on experiment analysis of 79 compositions, liquid fragility is found to consistently decreases under two conditions: i) when the alloying content x is minimal, irrespective of the elements used; or ii) when increasing the diversity of alloying elements at a constant x, namely the high‐entropy micro‐alloying. These observations are consistent with thermodynamic principles that favor an entropy‐dominated regime over enthalpy. These findings elucidate the subtle impact of mixing entropy on material properties and provide evidence of the entropy nature of glass transition. This research innovates by distinguishing entropy’s impact from enthalpy in materials through micro‐alloying. It finds liquid fragility decreases with minimal alloying content or increased element dive

Designing High Entropy Bulk Metallic Glass (HE-BMG) by Similar Element Substitution/Addition

Abstract: In this paper, we report that two newly designed high entropy bulk metallic glasses (HE-BMGs), Ti20Hf20Cu20Ni20Be20 with a critical diameter of 2 mm, and Ti16.7Zr16.7Nb16.7Cu16.7Ni16.7Be16.7 with a critical diameter of 1.5 mm, can be fabricated by copper mold casting method. These newly developed HE-BMGs exhibited a high fracture strength over 2300 MPa. The glass forming ability and atomic size distribution characteristics of the HE-BMGs are discussed in detail. Moreover, a parameter δ′ was proposed to evaluate the atomic size distribution characteristics in different HEAs. It showed that this new parameter is closely related to the degree of lattice distortion and phase selection of high-entropy alloys. Adjusting the value of δ′ parameter by similar element substitution/addition would be beneficial for designing high entropy bulk metallic glasses.
